name: 1-4-2 Ratio Breathing
scienceBlurb: This pattern places much more emphasis on breath retention than most everyday exercises. A different experience for comfortable practitioners, though longer holds aren't automatically better.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; longer holds not shown to be more effective.

name: 2-1-4-1 Breathing
scienceBlurb: Small counts and brief pauses make this an approachable way to practice controlled breathing. It's especially useful on days when longer patterns feel difficult to follow.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: 2-6 Calming Breath
scienceBlurb: A short inhale and a longer release create a deliberate, exhale-focused rhythm. Try it when you want to shift attention away from rushing and toward one breath at a time.
scienceBlurbSource: General slow-breathing research; not specific to 2-6

name: 3-3-6 Breathing
scienceBlurb: This pattern gives your exhale twice the time of your inhale or hold. Its simple structure makes it easier to concentrate on one breath rather than everything happening around you.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: 3-6 Breathing
scienceBlurb: Simple enough to remember anywhere, this pattern gives your exhale twice the time of your inhale. A useful rhythm when you want a pause without complicated counting.
scienceBlurbSource: General slow-breathing research; not specific to 3-6

name: 3-Part Yogic Breath
scienceBlurb: This practice guides your attention through the abdomen, ribs, and upper chest. It can help you notice the different movements involved in a full, comfortable breath.
scienceBlurbSource: American Lung Association — Related breathing anatomy guidance

name: 4-4-4 Triangle
scienceBlurb: Three equal phases make this easy to remember without looking at a screen. Try it as a small mental transition before studying, writing, or starting a focused task.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: 4-4-6-2 Breathing
scienceBlurb: Four phases and a longer exhale create a rhythm that asks for just enough attention to follow. A deliberate transition into focused work.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: 4-6 Breathing
scienceBlurb: Just a little longer out than in makes this an easy rhythm to remember. A practical everyday option for creating a calmer-feeling transition between activities.
scienceBlurbSource: General slow-breathing research; not specific to 4-6

name: 4-7-8 Breathing
scienceBlurb: Popularized by Dr. Andrew Weil and rooted in yogic breathing, this pattern is built for winding down. Its long, deliberate exhale makes it an easy ritual to remember when you want to slow your pace.
scienceBlurbSource: Andrew Weil — The Relaxing Breath

name: 4-8 Sleep Breathing
scienceBlurb: A longer exhale gives this pattern an unhurried bedtime rhythm. In a small sleep study, paced breathing before bed was linked to improvements in several sleep measures, though this exact ratio wasn't tested.
scienceBlurbSource: Tsai et al., 2015 — Related evidence: paced breathing before bed, not this exact ratio

name: 478 Variation
scienceBlurb: Inspired by the familiar 4-7-8 technique, this variation shortens the hold. It offers a more approachable introduction to the same style of counted breathing.
scienceBlurbSource: Andrew Weil — Original 4-7-8 technique

name: 5-5 Coherence Breathing
scienceBlurb: Five seconds in and five seconds out creates six breaths per minute, a pace commonly used in heart-rate variability research. A simple way to explore how breathing rhythm and heartbeat interact.
scienceBlurbSource: HRV Biofeedback Methods Review, 2023 — Six breaths per minute research pace

name: 6-2-7 Breathing
scienceBlurb: A measured inhale, short pause, and slightly longer exhale create a spacious rhythm. This pattern is best enjoyed without forcing the breath or rushing through the counts.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: 7-11 Breathing
scienceBlurb: This extended-exhale pattern gives you an unhurried rhythm to focus on. It's a practical way to settle into a longer pause between the demands of your day.
scienceBlurbSource: General slow-breathing research; not specific to 7-11

name: Alternate Nostril Breathing
scienceBlurb: This traditional yogic technique has been studied for cardiovascular effects. A 2024 review found promising blood-pressure reductions, though wide differences between studies limit how far the results generalize.
scienceBlurbSource: Nam et al., 2024 — Review; substantial differences between studies

name: Anti-Anxiety Breath
scienceBlurb: When anxious thoughts compete for attention, a predictable rhythm gives you something concrete to follow. Breathwork research suggests modest average stress benefits, though this exact pattern hasn't been independently studied.
scienceBlurbSource: Fincham et al., 2023 — General breathwork evidence; this exact pattern not studied

name: Belly Breathing
scienceBlurb: Your diaphragm is the main muscle behind every breath. Belly breathing helps you notice and use its movement, making it a useful skill for becoming more aware of how you breathe.
scienceBlurbSource: American Lung Association — Breathing exercise guidance

name: Bhramari (Humming Bee)
scienceBlurb: The soft hum gives you a soothing sound to focus on. In a study of 10 adults, humming raised measured nasal nitric oxide 15-fold compared with quiet exhalation — a fascinating effect of sound on sinus airflow.
scienceBlurbSource: Weitzberg & Lundberg, 2002 — Small study of 10 adults

name: Box Breathing
scienceBlurb: When your mind is busy, four predictable phases give you something steady to follow. Box breathing was one of the structured practices studied in a 2023 randomized breathwork trial.
scienceBlurbSource: Balban et al., 2023 — Box breathing was one of the practices studied

name: Breath of Fire
scienceBlurb: Rapid, rhythmic breathing is associated with Kundalini yoga. It offers a very different experience from slow breathing, but faster and more intense breathing isn't necessarily better, or right for everyone.
scienceBlurbSource: Traditional yogic practice; technique-specific reference pending verification.

name: Buteyko Breathing
scienceBlurb: Buteyko breathing emphasizes nasal breathing and reducing habitual overbreathing. Breathing-retraining methods, including Buteyko, have been studied in asthma care, with some evidence of improved quality of life.
scienceBlurbSource: Cochrane — Breathing exercises for asthma; some evidence of improved quality of life

name: Combat Tactical Breathing
scienceBlurb: A structured rhythm can give you a deliberate pause before a high-pressure moment. Its everyday value is simple: something predictable to follow when you want to stay composed.
scienceBlurbSource: General breathing guidance; military origin not asserted

name: Counting Breath
scienceBlurb: Counting gives wandering thoughts a place to land. An accessible way to practice returning to the present without needing to clear your mind completely.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation of mindfulness practice.

name: Cyclic Sighing
scienceBlurb: In a 2023 randomized study, five minutes of daily cyclic sighing over one month improved positive mood more than the mindfulness comparison and reduced breathing rate. A small practice with promising results.
scienceBlurbSource: Balban et al., 2023 — Randomized study of one month of daily practice

name: Energy Boost Breathing
scienceBlurb: A more active pattern offers a change from traditional relaxation exercises. A brief ritual for bringing attention to your body before your next activity — not a guaranteed energy boost.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: Equal Breathing (Sama Vritti)
scienceBlurb: Equal breathing creates a steady, predictable rhythm. A gentle way to give your attention something simple to follow as part of an evening wind-down routine.
scienceBlurbSource: General slow-breathing research; not specific to Sama Vritti

name: Extended Exhale
scienceBlurb: Giving your exhale more time can make a pause feel less hurried. Exhale-focused breathing was a key feature of cyclic sighing, which showed promising mood benefits in a 2023 study.
scienceBlurbSource: Balban et al., 2023 — Related evidence: cyclic sighing study, not this exact ratio

name: Grounding Breath
scienceBlurb: Grounding begins with something you can notice right now. Following your breath offers a repeatable point of attention when your thoughts feel scattered or overwhelming.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: Heart Coherence Breathing
scienceBlurb: Your heart rate naturally rises and falls with each breath. Slow, steady breathing makes that pattern easier to notice, offering an interesting way to explore the link between breath and heartbeat.
scienceBlurbSource: Laborde et al., 2022 — Related evidence on slow breathing and heart-rate variability

name: Kapalabhati (Skull Shining)
scienceBlurb: Unlike slower relaxation exercises, Kapalabhati uses rapid, active exhalations. A small physiological study observed changes in autonomic and brain-wave measures during practice, supporting its place as a more activating form of breathwork.
scienceBlurbSource: Kapalabhati Physiological Study, 2022 — Small physiological study

name: Lion's Breath
phaseLabels: inhale through nose,exhale through mouth wide
scienceBlurb: Not every breath needs to be quiet. This expressive yogic practice invites you to stretch your face, open your mouth, and exhale strongly — a playful way to explore releasing physical tension.
scienceBlurbSource: Traditional yogic practice; technique-specific reference pending verification.

name: Mindful Breath Awareness
scienceBlurb: You don't have to change your breath to practice mindfulness. Noticing when attention wanders and gently returning it to the breath is itself the whole skill.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation of mindfulness practice.

name: Morning Activation Breath
scienceBlurb: Not every breathing session has to be about slowing down. A more active rhythm can give your morning a deliberate starting point before you move into the day.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: Nadi Shodhana Advanced
scienceBlurb: Alternate-nostril breathing has attracted scientific interest alongside a long history in yoga. A review of randomized trials found promising blood-pressure results, though studies varied and advanced variations weren't shown to add benefit.
scienceBlurbSource: Nam et al., 2024 — Related evidence; advanced variations not shown to add benefit

name: Ocean Breathing (Ujjayi)
scienceBlurb: The gentle ocean-like sound becomes a natural point of focus. This traditional yogic technique makes breathing feel more immersive by giving you something to hear as well as feel.
scienceBlurbSource: Traditional yogic practice; technique-specific reference pending verification.

name: Panic Reset Breath
scienceBlurb: In an intense moment, simple instructions may feel more manageable than a complicated exercise. This pattern offers a gentle point of focus — not a treatment for panic attacks.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: Physiological Sigh
scienceBlurb: A double inhale followed by a longer exhale mirrors a sigh your body already does on its own. A quick, memorable pattern when you have only a moment to redirect your attention.
scienceBlurbSource: Balban et al., 2023 — Related evidence: cyclic sighing study, not this exact pattern

name: Power Breathing
scienceBlurb: This more demanding style explores a different side of breathwork: active breathing rather than quiet relaxation. Best approached as a controlled practice, not a challenge to breathe harder or hold longer.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: Pursed Lip Breathing
scienceBlurb: This technique has an established place in respiratory care. By slowing exhalation and helping airways stay open longer, it can help people with conditions such as COPD manage breathlessness.
scienceBlurbSource: American Lung Association — Guidance for COPD and breathlessness

name: Relaxing Breath
scienceBlurb: A shorter hold makes this variation more approachable than the traditional 4-7-8 pattern. It's a gentle way to explore structured breathing without committing to a longer pause.
scienceBlurbSource: Andrew Weil — Original 4-7-8 technique

name: Resonance Breathing
scienceBlurb: Breathing and heart rhythm are closely connected. Resonance breathing explores a pace where breathing-related heart-rate fluctuations become especially pronounced — and that pace can differ from person to person.
scienceBlurbSource: HRV Biofeedback Methods Review, 2023 — Resonance pace varies between individuals

name: Sitali Cooling Breath
scienceBlurb: Traditionally described as a cooling yogic breath, Sitali has a surprising scientific story: a small study found it didn't lower measured body temperature during practice. Its distinctive style still offers a refreshing change of pace.
scienceBlurbSource: Sheetali and Sitkari Temperature Study, 2020 — Small study; no measured drop in body temperature

name: Sleep Onset Breathing
scienceBlurb: Did you know? A small study found that practicing slow breathing for 20 minutes before bed was associated with better sleep. A gentle reminder that slowing down can be part of winding down.
scienceBlurbSource: Tsai et al., 2015 — Related paced-breathing research; the exact Sleep Onset Breathing pattern was not independently tested.

name: Slow Deep Breathing
scienceBlurb: A review of 223 studies found that voluntary slow breathing increased heart-rate variability measures linked to cardiac parasympathetic activity. Slowing down, it turns out, has real science behind it.
scienceBlurbSource: Laborde et al., 2022 — Review of 223 studies on slow breathing and heart-rate variability

name: Straw Breathing
scienceBlurb: Breathing out through a narrow opening creates gentle resistance and encourages a controlled exhale — the same principle behind pursed-lip breathing, used to ease breathlessness.
scienceBlurbSource: American Lung Association — Related clinical guidance

name: Triangle Breathing
scienceBlurb: A repeating three-part pattern gives your mind one simple job. A useful option when you'd like to collect your thoughts before moving on to the next task.
scienceBlurbSource: Descriptive explanation; no technique-specific clinical claim.

name: Tummo Inner Fire
scienceBlurb: Tummo combines specialized breathing with meditative visualization. In a 2013 study, experienced practitioners showed measurable increases in body temperature during certain forms of the practice — a remarkable example of mind-body research.
scienceBlurbSource: Kozhevnikov et al., 2013 — Study of experienced practitioners

name: Vagal Toning Breath
scienceBlurb: The vagus nerve helps regulate automatic functions, including heart activity. Slow breathing can increase measures of cardiac vagal activity, but lasting benefits from this exact routine haven't been established.
scienceBlurbSource: Laborde et al., 2022 — Related evidence; lasting change from this exact routine not established

name: Wim Hof Breathing
scienceBlurb: Researchers studied a program combining intensive breathing, cold exposure, and meditation. A small randomized trial found changes in immune responses, but it doesn't establish that breathing alone produced those effects.
scienceBlurbSource: Kox et al., 2014 — Small randomized study of a combined breathing, cold, and meditation program
